# 13-aircaps: sources

Back-test entry `13-aircaps.yaml`. AirCaps, YC Fall 2025 (Launch YC 2025-11-05). Read 2026-10-22.

Sources (short names used below):

- **SITE**: https://www.aircaps.com (testimonials, pricing, how it works)
- **YC-L**: Launch YC post. https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/Olk-aircaps-the-ai-copilot-for-in-person-conversations
- **YC-C**: YC company page. https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/aircaps
- **YALE**: Yale Alumni Magazine. https://yalealumnimagazine.org/articles/6208
- **SD**: Stanford Daily, 2023-02-06 (TranscribeGlass). https://stanforddaily.com/2023/02/06/stanford-startup-transcribeglass-seeks-to-bring-ease-and-affordability-to-assistive-technology/
- **SMI**: Smithsonian Magazine. https://www.smithsonianmag.com/innovation/this-augmented-reality-tool-could-change-communication-for-some-deaf-and-hearing-impaired-people-180982996/
- **T4G**: Tech4Good Awards finalist entry. https://tech4goodawards.com/finalist/transcribeglass/ (quoted through the shortlist; not re-fetched)
- **HT**: HearingTracker, "Hear with Your Eyes: A Review of Live Captioning Glasses". https://www.hearingtracker.com/hearing-glasses/hear-with-your-eyes-five-ar-live-captioning-glasses
- **DTS-ASL**: ASL Deafined blog, "Dinner Table Syndrome: What Deaf, DeafBlind, and Hard of Hearing People Face". https://blog.asldeafined.com/2025/05/dinner-table-syndrome-what-deaf-deafblind-and-hard-of-hearing-people-face/

**Caution:** the origin story comes from the founder's earlier device, TranscribeGlass (about 2017 to 2023), which predates the YC batch. Here it is the founder's own account of where the problem came from, not evidence about AirCaps' buyers.

## The eight founder-emulation items

**1. Who (the CONSUMER role, `wearer`; context actor).**
- T4G (through the shortlist): a hard-of-hearing friend who "dropped out of school because day-to-day communication with other students was becoming an insurmountable problem".
- SMI: the friend "found it difficult to understand what teachers and even his friends were saying."
- YALE: the founder began at 16, after a hard-of-hearing classmate in Delhi left school because hearing aids alone did not let him follow his teachers (as read).
- SITE, "Who it's for": "Deaf and Hard of Hearing people" first, then travelers, multilingual families and professionals.

**2. What (the job).**
- YC-L: phones break eye contact and earbuds confuse the audio (as read), so face-to-face conversations get no captions.
- SITE: a private display in the lenses shows the text, visible only to the wearer (as read).
- Job wording ("follow and join a face-to-face conversation") is mine, from these two.

**3. When / where (circumstance, occasion, window).**
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "When I was sitting around a table, I lost the conversation".
- SD (co-founder with hearing loss): "my understanding drops to 20% at best" in group conversations, where he mostly nods along.
- SMI: "Hearing aids aren't dependable in a lot of situations, especially ones with a lot of background noise."
- *My choice:* occasion "group conversation"; window 7 days; Frequency 4 to 7 days out of 7. That rests on YC-L's power users (6+ hours of daily use, as read) and the ordinary weekly rhythm of meals, work and family.

**4. Which people (segment, market).**
- SITE lists deaf and hard-of-hearing people first. YC-L also names meeting-heavy professionals.
- YALE: a Deaf ASL instructor who does not speak sees the glasses as one-directional.
- *My choice:* the segment is narrowed to "deaf and hard-of-hearing adults in the US who talk with hearing people every week". This is the day-one wedge the origin story points at, and the travellers and professionals came later. Market US: the testimonials and HSA/FSA are US.

**5. Who pays (Buyer and payer).**
- SITE: "HSA/FSA eligible" (as read). One testimonial is from a daughter about her father joining family conversations.
- *My choice:* the wearer decides and pays, and nobody else has to agree (Nobody else, picked).

**6. Mechanism (solution statement, solution_mechanism, compatibility and adoption items).**
- YC-L: captions and notes "displayed on lightweight AR glasses" (as read).
- SITE: four microphones capture nearby speech; the glasses "require a Bluetooth connection to a phone and an internet connection" (as read).
- Compatibility tests "Their phone was with them and online", because the mechanism needs both. Adoption friction tests "Wear the glasses, paired to the phone". Both are my choices from these facts.
- Commitment step "order a pair with free returns": SITE, "15-day risk-free returns".

**7. Price (Price, Existing sacrifice, Ability to pay).**
- SITE: glasses "Starting at $599"; free plan with unlimited captions; "Pro plan: $20/month".
- YALE: "which cost $649 in early 2026". HT's table: "$499 / $699 (Premium $20/mth)".
- *My choice:* the price is put on a year, because the ladder has no one-off: **$599 to $839 a year**. That is the glasses with free captions, up to the glasses plus twelve months of Pro.
- *My choice:* the cost estimate (Existing sacrifice) is **$200 to $1,500 a year**, from the commercial statement's "many already pay for captioning apps and hearing-aid extras". No source gives a figure. SMI notes hearing aids are "often costing thousands of dollars", so the high end stops short of a hearing aid itself. Ability to pay is derived by code: 40% to 420%, some from spend.

**8. Occasions (statements, gate, stories).**
- SITE testimonials: "I could start going to the theatre again"; "With AirCaps I can follow almost all" (at a table with friends); "I can attend speeches and seminars in large spaces and understand words"; a testimonial about an uncaptioned movie theater; one about a father following family conversations.
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups".
- YALE: a first-year deaf in one ear followed three friends in a noisy café. A largely deaf professor found the captions "messing up" at a screening, and they kept him in the loop on a walk drowned by construction noise.

## The respondents

No respondent carries a real person's name; every name is invented. Where a story follows a public account, the occasion is borrowed and the person is not.

- Harriet Coleman: SITE theatre testimonial ("I could start going to the theatre again").
- Walter Nguyen: shortlist reading of SITE ("My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups") and the SITE family-conversation testimonial.
- Diego Herrera: SITE table-with-friends testimonial; DTS-ASL ("if others are facing away or talking too quickly, these visual cues can be lost").
- Amaka Obi: YC-L (phones break eye contact); SMI (phone subtitles leave users "stuck looking at their screens at all times"); SITE work testimonial.
- Ruth Feldman: SITE testimonial on "speeches and seminars in large spaces".
- Tomás Reyes: YALE, the first-year deaf in one ear with three friends in a café.
- Eleanor Park: YALE, the campus walk where construction noise nearly drowned the conversation.
- Colette Marchand: SITE testimonial on an uncaptioned movie theater; YALE screening.
- Andrea Whitlock: YALE, the Deaf ASL instructor who sees the glasses as one-directional and worries institutions could cut services. She is the sceptic who will not adopt.
- Gordon McBride: author's invention, filling a gap: a hearing-aid user whose quiet week went fine, the low-frequency case. It is the other side of SMI's "aren't dependable ... with a lot of background noise".
- Kwame Asante: SD (bars: "I have a really hard time"; "my understanding drops to 20% at best", nodding along).
- Shirin Tehrani: SMI, the late-deafened user who relies "completely on live transcription and captions" and names doctor visits.
- Beatriz Souza: SMI ("Since the app needs the speaker to converse in English, I have not been able to use it much in social settings").
- Hollis Grant: author's invention, filling a gap: a vague, unanchored story so the entry carries one GUESSED reading.
- Naomi Adler: author's invention, filling a gap: a chipped story (rather not say). DTS-ASL on "frustration, anxiety, and even a reluctance to attend social events".
- Frank Dellinger: DTS-ASL (family dinners and gatherings, "talking over each other").
- Ingrid Solberg: author's invention, filling a gap: a counter conversation through a screen and a mask, where lipreading fails. DTS-ASL on lost visual cues.
- Patrick Moran: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No (a quiet week with no hard conversation).
- Lucia Ferraro: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.
- Desmond Hale: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.

## Open

- **The origin story predates the batch.** It is TranscribeGlass's. The day-one founder statements use it as the founders do in the press, but a back-test should weigh it as the founder's lived reason, not as customer evidence.
- **Price conflict.** SITE says $599, YALE $649 (early 2026), and HT $499 / $699. I used SITE's $599, as the price the founder would type today. The year framing ($599 to $839) is mine.
- **The cost estimate is mine.** $200 to $1,500 a year has no public figure behind it. The commercial vector's NOT_HOLDING_UP comes mostly from people who spend nothing today (free phone captions), against that estimate.
- **Two shortlist quotes not re-seen.** My fetch of SITE did not return the "sitting around a table, I lost the conversation" and "My wife appreciates..." quotes verbatim, though it did return the other testimonials. They are cited through the shortlist. The site may rotate testimonials.
- **Relative advantage code.** keel-cloud's `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` accepts only five legacy advantage codes. The benefit is labelled "Following more without asking anyone to repeat" under the nearest code, `less_help_needed`.
- **Checker result.** `instructions/corpus.py` (keel-e2e-eval) loads the file with the registry bound and raises no refusal. `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` reports only "missing top-level 'expected'", which is intentional. Its recount, which is not a golden: PROBLEM PEOPLE_DISAGREE (Frequency: many have it 2 to 3 days a week, not 4 to 7), SOLUTION HOLDING_UP, COMMERCIAL NOT_HOLDING_UP (Existing sacrifice).

whys.g1: The name is plain, but Colette's answer is mainly about the venue not allowing the phone and having no signal, which is a different barrier from Frank's flat battery, so 'off or dead' stretches to hold her.
whys.g2: There is no junk answer on this line; both answers are about what stops the phone from being used.

insights.line: What would have made a difference

whys.g1: Both answers are about phone calls and keeping up in live talk rather than reading captions, so putting them together makes sense to me and "Calls and answering back" is plain, though it leaves out Gordon's point about being worn out after a day of listening.
whys.g2: There is no junk or off-topic answer on this line; both are real answers about what would help.

whys.g1: Gordon McBride and Andrea Whitlock are put under "I manage well enough already", but both are saying the hard part is somewhere else (phone calls and the tiredness after a day of listening; answering back in meetings), not that they are managing fine; that is a group they do not belong in, even though Tomás and Ingrid fit it and the other two groups read plainly.
whys.g2: There is no junk, explicit or off-topic answer on this line; every answer speaks to what would make the glasses too much or worth more.

founder.order_why: It runs from where I sell, to the context, to the problem my wearers have, to my glasses and how they fit, beat and start, and only then to the pilot and who gets a link, which is the order I would explain AirCaps in.
founder.asked_twice: Screens 3 and 4 carry the same question word for word ('Before we test anything, let's define exactly where this idea applies'); if they hold different context fields that's fine, but as listed it reads as the same question asked twice.
founder.missing: Nothing asks whether the people I talk to speak and lipread or sign. A Deaf ASL user who doesn't voice can read captions but can't answer back, so the glasses only work one way for them. Nothing asks what language the hearing side speaks either, and captions that only handle English fail in multilingual settings. Both decide whether a stranger in my segment can use the glasses at all.

PRIMARY.order_why: Asking whether my phone was with me and online comes before I'm even asked if AirCaps would have helped, which feels like a setup question in an odd spot rather than following from the idea itself.
PRIMARY.missing: Nothing about how I manage now — lipreading, asking people to repeat, a captioning app, hearing aids, or an interpreter — or what the struggle actually cost me in that conversation, like dropping out of it or leaving early.

screens.why4: The interviewer face comes preselected and locked, but for deaf and hard-of-hearing respondents the real question is whether the AI interviewer is captioned or text-only; the choices don't say so, and that answer decides it for my people.
screens.why5: Nothing of my study's wording or my product is altered or leaked here; it only picks the interviewer.
screens.instead: Who asks your questions? My people are deaf and hard of hearing, so: an AI interviewer they read, all in text (uses Keel credits) / a link I send myself, text only / I'll ask them myself

screens.why1: Choosing how strangers answer belongs right before sending, after the pilot and who-asks screens.
screens.why2: The AI interviewer line has a sound-engineering claim, "More than 90% in loud places down to 5 dB", which I can't read on first pass (5 dB of what?), and it runs into "Hear it" with no space.
screens.why3: I know my wearers are deaf and hard-of-hearing, so I can tell at once that answering by reading and tapping fits them.
screens.why4: The three choices are distinct and Text only covers my case, but the AI interviewer option says only that questions are asked aloud and doesn't say they are captioned, which matters for my respondents.
screens.why5: Nothing of my product or roles leaks, and my pick of Text only is kept as typed.
screens.instead: How should they answer? -- AI interviewer (a face on video asks each question aloud, with captions on screen; they talk or tap; needs Keel's credits) / Text only (they read each question and tap) / Let them choose (both offered when they open the link; needs Keel's credits)

screens.why1: Once the interviews are set to send, choosing who receives a link is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: 'Someone I know' is plain, but 'People from a dataset … found on Contacts' needs a second read: I don't know what 'Contacts' is here or what Keel found, and 'dataset' isn't how I'd describe the deaf and hard-of-hearing people I talk to.
screens.why3: I know who I can reach: the hard-of-hearing people in my network, our waitlist and the HLAA-type groups, so I can answer this from what I actually have.
screens.why4: The two options are distinct, but a common real route is missing: an open link I post in a community or group or send to our waitlist. The second option's wording is also murky.
screens.why5: Nothing of the study's meaning changes, and nothing about the glasses or the roles leaks to the people being sent the link.
screens.instead: Who gets a link? — People I know, each by name / An open link I post or share with a group or waitlist / People Keel finds for me (say from where)

screens.why1: As the first screen it makes sense to check that I talk with hearing people at all before asking about those conversations, though the kicker says 'a recent time' while the question asks about a weekly habit.
screens.why2: 'Hearing people' is how I and other deaf people talk about them, so I understand it on first read.
screens.why3: I know whether I talk with hearing people each week: at work, in shops, with family.
screens.why4: Yes or No covers a gate question, and having no escape fits a screener.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's segment of people who talk with hearing people every week, and nothing about a product or plan reaches me.
screens.why6: It is short and is one question, though 'I'll read 2 options' before a plain yes or no is a little stiff.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, did you talk face to face with a hearing person? Yes; or No.

screens.why1: Right after confirming I talk with hearing people every week, asking whether I struggled to follow one of those conversations this past week is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: "Struggle to follow a conversation with hearing people" is exactly how I and other deaf people talk about it, so I can answer straight away.
screens.why3: I know whether I lost the thread at work, in a shop or at dinner this week; it's my own life.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it, but the screen shows two escapes on a gate that should have none, and "I'd rather not say" is one the rules say does not exist; "I can't recall one particular conversation" also doesn't fit, because the question asks about the whole week, not one conversation.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's job and circumstance, and nothing about a product or the founder's own terms reaches me.
screens.why6: Spoken as "In the last 7 days, did you struggle to follow a conversation with hearing people? Yes or no." it is one short question I can hear once and answer.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, did you struggle to follow a conversation with hearing people? Yes / No (no escape chip on this gate)

screens.why1: After asking whether I struggled to follow a conversation this week, showing me an idea for exactly that moment makes obvious sense as the start of part 2.
screens.why2: Glasses, an app, live captions in the lens, eye contact -- captions is a word I use every day, and all of it reads plainly first time.
screens.why3: Fast or noisy conversations where I lose the thread and have to choose between lipreading and reading a phone screen are my life, so I can picture this straight away.
screens.why4: A card to read, no options shown.
screens.why5: It is an idea card shown on purpose, in plain words, with no roles or internal terms leaking -- the product name is offered as the thing to imagine.
screens.why6: Said aloud it is four sentences with a long middle one ('The app turns what the people nearby are saying into written words and shows them as live captions inside the lens'), a mouthful to hold in one hearing -- and read aloud to a deaf person, it should also be on screen as text, which it is.
screens.instead: Imagine AirCaps. When a conversation is too fast or too noisy, you wear light glasses. They show what people nearby say as live captions in the lens. The people building it believe you could read the words and still keep eye contact.

screens.why1: Right after the question about my last conversation and the idea card, asking whether AirCaps would have helped there is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: It is short and plain, and I would know at once whether captions would have helped me in that conversation.
screens.why3: I was in that conversation and know how much I missed, so I can judge whether captions would have changed it.
screens.why4: "Following more without asking anyone to repeat" is not a separate answer but one way of "made things better", so the two overlap and the list stops being a clean better / no difference / worse scale.
screens.why5: The question keeps the founder's meaning, but the benefit line reads like the founder's pitch slipped into my answers, nudging me towards "better".
screens.why6: Spoken, the odd second option breaks the better / no difference / worse pattern, so I would have to hold a different kind of phrase in the middle of the list.
screens.instead: Thinking of that conversation, would AirCaps have made it better, or not? It would have made it better; No difference; or It would have made it worse. Or say I can't tell.

screens.why1: After asking whether AirCaps would have helped, it makes sense to ask whether I would actually wear the glasses in conversations.
screens.why2: Wearing glasses paired to my phone during conversations is plain to me, and I can answer straight away.
screens.why3: I know whether I would put on captioning glasses when I'm talking with hearing people at work, at the shops or at the theatre bar.
screens.why4: The options lean toward no: there is 'Yes, if it was clearly worth it' but no 'Probably yes', and 'clearly worth it' mostly repeats the last question, so the middle of the scale is uneven.
screens.why5: It asks about wearing the glasses with my phone, which is what the idea card showed me, and none of the founder's own terms for people come through.
screens.why6: It is short, says one thing and then asks one question, and four short options plus 'I can't tell' are easy to hold when heard once.
screens.instead: Would you wear the AirCaps glasses, paired to your phone, in your conversations with hearing people, or not? Yes, every time; Yes, some of the time; Probably not; No — or say I can't tell.

screens.why1: Right after asking whether I'd wear the glasses paired to my phone, it makes sense to ask what would tip it for me.
screens.why2: It's short, but 'it' could mean the glasses, the money or the hassle of wearing them, so I'd have to think back two screens to be sure.
screens.why3: I know what would make captions worth it for me, like keeping up at a noisy dinner, the captions being fast and right, and the glasses not looking odd, so I can answer from my own life.
screens.why4: It's a box to type in with no options.
screens.why5: It stays on the idea already shown on the card and adds no new product talk or labels for me.
screens.why6: One short question with nothing to hold in my head, easy to hear once and answer.
screens.instead: What would make wearing captioning glasses in conversations clearly worth it to you?
